THOUGHT: This is an elderly woman with subacute cognitive/behavioral change progressing to severe consciousness disturbance and large focal deficits, and imaging showing abundant lobar microbleeds and macrobleeds on SWI and "bleeding throughout the brain" on CT. The lobar distribution of microbleeds/macrobleeds on a 3‑T SWI in an older patient is characteristic of cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA). The CSF shows markedly reduced Aβ40 and a low Aβ40/Aβ42 ratio relative to reported normals, which supports cortical vascular amyloid deposition (CAA is associated with reduced CSF Aβ40 and Aβ42). She also has severe thrombocytopenia from immune thrombocytopenic purpura (platelets <5×10^3/µL), which by itself greatly increases risk of diffuse intracranial hemorrhage and would worsen any CAA-related bleeding. CAA-related inflammation (CAA‑ri) can present with subacute cognitive decline, but typically shows MRI confluent T2/FLAIR white‑matter hyperintensity/edema and inflammatory CSF changes, which are not described here. Deep hypertensive arteriolosclerosis usually produces deep (basal ganglia/thalamic) hemorrhages rather than the lobar pattern seen here. Cerebral venous thrombosis or hemorrhagic metastases are less consistent with the imaging pattern and biomarker profile.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) with multiple lobar intracerebral hemorrhages and microbleeds (most likely cause of the imaging pattern and supported by low CSF Aβ40 and low Aβ40/Aβ42 ratio)
2. Intracerebral hemorrhage secondary to severe thrombocytopenia from immune thrombocytopenic purpura (diffuse hemorrhagic complications exacerbating extent/severity)
3. Combined/overlapping CAA plus severe thrombocytopenia–related intracranial hemorrhage (synergistic cause of massive, widespread lobar bleeding)
4. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy–related inflammation (CAA‑ri) presenting with subacute cognitive decline and hemorrhagic lesions (less likely given absent described MRI/CSF inflammatory features)
5. Hypertensive small‑vessel (arteriolosclerotic) intracerebral hemorrhage or multifocal hemorrhagic lesions from other causes (e.g., hemorrhagic metastatic disease or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis) — less likely based on lobar predominant SWI findings and CSF amyloid profile
